title: Freeze Warnings Just Hit the Gulf Coast — If Your Balcony Has Citrus or Bougainvillea on It, Act Before Tonight
intro: The National Weather Service issued a string of freeze warnings and freeze watches late Thanksgiving night into Friday morning across the Gulf South: a freeze warning for George, Greene, Perry, and Stone counties in Mississippi (lows near 31°F from roughly 3 to 7 a.m. CST), freeze warnings for central and southwest Louisiana and far east Texas — Avoyelles, Evangeline, Rapides, St. Landry, Allen, Beauregard, and Vernon Parishes plus northern Jasper, Newton, and Tyler counties in Texas — and a freeze watch covering West Feliciana, East Feliciana, St. Helena, and roughly a dozen more southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi parishes and counties for Friday night into Saturday morning. Baton Rouge-area forecasters at WBRZ are already flagging that a repeat watch or warning is likely for Saturday night into Sunday as well. This matters specifically for apartment and condo growers in this region because it's a different kind of cold event than the ones we've covered in Minneapolis, Omaha, or the Mid-Atlantic this fall: those are zone 5-7 areas where balcony plants are already cold-hardy perennials. The Gulf South is zone 8-9. A huge share of balcony and patio containers down here are things that have never once seen a hard freeze — citrus, bougainvillea, tropical hibiscus, bird of paradise, elephant ears — and most renters in Baton Rouge, Lafayette, Hattiesburg, or Beaumont simply don't own frost cloth or a plant dolly because they've never needed one before this week.

sections.heading: Why this freeze is a bigger deal for Gulf South balconies than for anyone further north
sections.body: A 31-33°F low for a few hours is background noise to a Minneapolis balcony garden — everything on it is already dormant or indoors. It's a different problem in Baton Rouge, New Orleans's suburbs, or coastal Mississippi, where the growing season barely pauses and the plants people keep on patios and balconies skew tropical and subtropical: potted citrus, bougainvillea, hibiscus, elephant ears, bird of paradise, even bananas. None of those have meaningful cold tolerance — citrus can show leaf damage in the low 30s and real wood damage below 28°F, and tropicals like elephant ears and bananas can lose their above-ground growth outright at a hard freeze. Because this kind of warning is rare here, most apartment and condo growers in the warning zone don't own the gear a northern grower already has on hand: frost cloth, a soil thermometer, or even a plan for where a four-foot citrus tree in a pot actually goes when it can't go in a garage. The forecast window is short — a few hours before dawn — but short doesn't mean survivable without doing anything.

products.name: Agfabric frost blanket plant cover
products.blurb: A reusable floating frost blanket draped over citrus, hibiscus, or bougainvillea and clipped or weighted at the base traps enough ground heat to get a potted tropical through a few hours in the low 30s, which is exactly the duration in tonight's and Saturday night's warnings.
products.priceNote: Sold by size; a single large sheet is enough to cover one good-sized patio citrus tree or several smaller pots grouped together.

products.name: Rolling plant caddy / plant dolly with wheels
products.blurb: The actual blocker for a lot of renters isn't knowing a freeze is coming, it's that a potted citrus or banana is too heavy to carry through a doorway alone — a wheeled plant caddy lets you stage it near the threshold in minutes and roll it in instead of attempting a last-minute two-person lift in the dark.
products.priceNote: A heavy-duty caddy rated for 100+ lbs is worth the extra cost if you're moving anything citrus-sized more than once a winter.
products.searchQuery: rolling plant caddy dolly with wheels heavy duty

sections.heading: What to actually do tonight versus what can wait
sections.body: Move what you can move: anything in a pot under about 15 inches across — hibiscus, smaller bougainvillea, elephant ear divisions — comes inside, into a garage, or at minimum tight against an exterior wall under a covered patio where it's shielded from radiational cooling. For anything too large or too heavy to move, water the soil before the cold arrives (moist soil holds heat better than dry soil overnight) and cover the whole plant down to the ground with frost cloth or, in a pinch, a sheet or moving blanket — the point is trapping the heat radiating up from the ground, not insulating the plant from the air. Don't use plastic sheeting directly against foliage; it conducts cold and can do more damage than no cover at all where it touches leaves. Uncover everything once temperatures climb back above freezing in the morning, since trapped humidity under a cover in full sun is its own problem. Given that WBRZ's own forecasters expect this to repeat Saturday night, this isn't a one-off scramble — anyone in the warning or watch zones is going to want frost cloth and a plan in place for the rest of the weekend, not just tonight.

products.name: ThermoPro wireless indoor/outdoor thermometer
products.blurb: A cheap wireless sensor clipped near your covered plants tells you the actual temperature at plant level overnight instead of guessing from a citywide forecast — useful this weekend specifically since the watch zones are borderline (32-33°F) and the warning zones are a few degrees colder.
products.priceNote: Basic two-piece wireless kits are inexpensive and reusable all winter, not just for this event.

conclusion: If you're an apartment or condo grower anywhere in the Mississippi, Louisiana, or east Texas counties under tonight's or Saturday's freeze warnings and watches, the move is the same regardless of which specific parish you're in: bring in what's small enough to carry now, water and cover what's too big to move, and don't assume a few hours in the low 30s is harmless just because it's short — tropical and subtropical container plants don't have the cold tolerance that makes a brief dip a non-event further north. And because the local forecast pattern points to this repeating into the weekend, it's worth treating tonight as the reason to actually buy frost cloth and a plant dolly rather than borrowing a neighbor's sheet one more time.
